question_text: If progress in increasing $T_c$ for superconductors had continued at the linear rate followed through 1975, by what year would a $T_c$ of 95 K be achieved? Give your answer as the value of year.
response:
Based on my analysis, this is a classic materials science problem that requires fitting a linear trend to the historical superconductor $T_c$ record data up to 1975 and extrapolating to find when $T_c = 95$ K would be reached.

## Approach

The historical record-high $T_c$ values through 1975 are:

| Year | Material | $T_c$ (K) |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 1911 | Hg | 4.2 |
| 1913 | Pb | 7.2 |
| 1929 | Nb | 9.2 |
| 1941 | NbN | 15.0 |
| 1953 | V₃Si | 17.1 |
| 1954 | Nb₃Sn | 18.1 |
| 1962 | — | 18.5 |
| 1968 | — | 20.8 |
| 1973 | Nb₃Ge | 23.2 |

**Step 1: Fit a linear trend** $T_c = a + b \cdot \text{year}$ using least-squares regression through these data points.

**Step 2: Solve for the year when $T_c = 95$ K.**

## Calculation

The linear regression yields:
- Slope: $b \approx 0.2802$ K/year  
- Intercept: $a \approx -530.18$

Setting $T_c = 95$ K:

$$95 = -530.18 + 0.2802 \times \text{year}$$

$$\text{year} = \frac{95 + 530.18}{0.2802} \approx 2231$$

This result makes physical sense: the pre-1975 rate of progress was only ~0.28 K/year, so reaching 95 K would have taken until well beyond the 22nd century. The actual discovery of 95 K superconductors (YBCO, 1987) represented a dramatic acceleration far exceeding this historical linear trend — precisely the point of the problem.

$$\boxed{2231}$$
